\chapter{Noon and Midnight}
\label{ch:ka-noon-and-midnight}
\hlchaptermodality{17}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say noon and midnight in Kannada and point out the \textquotedblleft{}middle\textquotedblright{} word they share.}

Say \kn{ಮಧ್ಯಾಹ್ನ} and \kn{ಮಧ್ಯರಾತ್ರಿ}, then isolate the madhya sitting inside both.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[madhyāhna madhyarātri]{\kn{ಮಧ್ಯಾಹ್ನ}, \kn{ಮಧ್ಯರಾತ್ರಿ} — one Sanskrit root, two everyday Kannada words}

\label{lesson:KA-C17-madhyaahna-madhyaraatri}



\begin{quote}
You've just seen Hindi's \emph{dopahar} (an old timekeeping unit) and \emph{aadhi raat} (plain \textquotedblleft{}half night\textquotedblright{}). Kannada takes a completely different path — straight to Sanskrit, and straight down the middle.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\kn{ಮಧ್ಯಾಹ್ನ}} (\emph{madhyāhna}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{noon, midday}\textquotedblright{} — a Sanskrit \emph{tatsama} (borrowed whole, unchanged) compound: \textbf{\kn{ಮಧ್ಯ}} (\emph{madhya}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{middle}\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{\kn{ಅಹ್ನ}} (\emph{ahna}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{day}\textquotedblright{}). This is the everyday, ordinary Kannada word for noon — not a formal or bookish alternative the way it can feel in some of its sister languages.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\kn{ಮಧ್ಯರಾತ್ರಿ}} (\emph{madhyarātri}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{midnight}\textquotedblright{} — the exact same \textbf{\kn{ಮಧ್ಯ}} (\emph{madhya}, \textquotedblleft{}middle\textquotedblright{}) root, this time compounded with \textbf{\kn{ರಾತ್ರಿ}} (\emph{rātri}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{night}\textquotedblright{}). Same logic, same \textquotedblleft{}middle\textquotedblright{} word, just paired with \textquotedblleft{}night\textquotedblright{} instead of \textquotedblleft{}day.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
Both words are unmistakably \textbf{Sanskrit tatsama} compounds — Kannada borrowed them whole rather than building native Dravidian equivalents. That's worth contrasting directly with Hindi, a language actually \emph{descended} from Sanskrit: Hindi has these exact same words too (\emph{madhyāhna}, \emph{madhyarātri}), but treats them as the more \textbf{formal, literary} register — its everyday words are the homegrown \emph{dopahar} (\textquotedblleft{}two pahars\textquotedblright{}) and \emph{aadhi raat} (\textquotedblleft{}half night\textquotedblright{}) instead. Kannada, by contrast, took the Sanskrit-formal compound and made it the \textbf{plain, everyday} word — there's no separate native-Dravidian doublet in common use here the way there is for some other concepts.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}madhyāhna\textquotedblright{} — noon, \textquotedblleft{}middle of the day\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}madhyarātri\textquotedblright{} — midnight, \textquotedblleft{}middle of the night\textquotedblright{}
  \item the shared piece — \textquotedblleft{}madhya,\textquotedblright{} middle, in both words
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What Sanskrit root do \textbf{\kn{ಮಧ್ಯಾಹ್ನ}} and \textbf{\kn{ಮಧ್ಯರಾತ್ರಿ}} share, and what does it mean? (\textbf{\kn{ಮಧ್ಯ}}, \emph{madhya}, \textquotedblleft{}middle.\textquotedblright{}) Are these native Dravidian words or Sanskrit borrowings? (\textbf{Sanskrit tatsama} borrowings, taken whole.) Does Hindi treat its version of these words as everyday or formal? (\textbf{Formal/literary} — Hindi's everyday words are \emph{dopahar} and \emph{aadhi raat} instead.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[9]{\kn{೯} — the digit for ombattu}

\label{lesson:KA-S148-digit-nine}



\begin{quote}
Before the new shape: \textbf{\kn{೮}} — which number is it?

One digit this time, and you already know its name.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \kn{೯}}
\textbf{\kn{೯}} — \textbf{9}, the digit for \textbf{\kn{ಒಂಬತ್ತು}} (\emph{ombattu}), \textquotedblleft{}nine\textquotedblright{}.

Nine — the last of the shapes that stand alone. One more to go, and it is the one that makes every larger number possible.

\subsection*{Writing: \kn{೯} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \kn{೯} and follow its line. Copy the shape in front of you — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what you can see needs no such source.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at the digits you have met, and name each one aloud
\end{itemize}

\kn{೧}  ·  \kn{೨}  ·  \kn{೩}  ·  \kn{೪}  ·  \kn{೫}  ·  \kn{೬}  ·  \kn{೭}  ·  \kn{೮}  ·  \kn{೯}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
